subtitle: Announcing the new Telnet options from RFC 651 to 658.

tldr.problem: Multiple new Telnet options had been defined in RFCs 651 to 658, but there was no central announcement to notify the community and point to the official list.
tldr.mechanism: This is a short announcement document that lists the new options and points to where they are defined: a revised Status option (RFC 651) and seven new options for handling formatting characters like tabs, formfeeds, and line-feeds.
tldr.outcome: The community was notified of the options and could refer to the individual RFCs for the technical specifications. These options were included in the official Telnet protocol suite.

today: RFC 659 is an announcement of RFCs 651 through 658. The options it announced are Historic; they are no longer widely used, as modern Telnet implementations handle formatting characters differently or not at all.

sections.title: The Telnet Options Announcement
sections.content: RFC 659 is a short announcement document by Jon Postel at SRI-ARC, written to draw attention to a new set of Telnet options that had been defined in RFCs 651 through 658. It does not define any protocol itself; it simply announces the official adoption of these options into the Telnet protocol and directs readers to the documents where the actual specifications are found.
sections.eli5: This is just a notice: some new Telnet options have been written down in other RFCs, and here is where to find them.

sections.title: The Options Being Announced
sections.content: RFC 651 is a revision of the existing Status option, redesigned to use the Telnet subcommand feature and reduce the number of bits needed for the status information. RFCs 652 through 658 define seven entirely new options for controlling format effector characters—characters that control how text is displayed on terminals and printers. These characters are carriage return, horizontal tab, formfeed, vertical tab, and line-feed. The new options allow the two ends of a Telnet connection to negotiate how each character should be handled.
sections.eli5: One of the options revises an old rule about status checking. Seven new options let two computers agree on what to do with special characters that control text formatting.

sections.title: Where to Find the Specifications
sections.content: The RFC lists online file locations where the documentation is available (from ISI and SRI-ARC systems), noting that at the time, the Network Information Center could not provide hardcopy and the author was responsible for distribution. The reference to RFC 645, "Network Standard Data Specification Syntax," notes that important document had not received wide circulation and points interested readers to it as well.
sections.eli5: Here is where to find the actual documents: these online file names point to the full specifications for all eight new options.
